content: On August 7, August 28, September 16, October 6, and November 5, meetings were held with the Guideline Development Group (GDG) to discuss the scope of the guidelines, the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions, the scoring of outcomes, and the progress of evidence reviews in preparation for the main meeting. For certain sessions, evidence-assessment groups were invited to participate as resource persons. Between these webinars, discussions continued via email. Additionally, two WebEx discussions were conducted in 2015 with members of the External Review Group (ERG) on September 7 and October 29 to brief them on their roles and expectations as peer reviewers. The 2016 update of the WHO treatment guidelines for drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) recommended the use of rapid drug susceptibility testing (DST) for at least rifampicin in adults and children at the time of TB diagnosis, as opposed to conventional testing or no testing. This was a strong recommendation based on high-certainty evidence. For patients with rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) or multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) who had not been previously treated with second-line drugs and were unlikely to have resistance to fluoroquinolones or second-line injectable agents, a shorter MDR-TB treatment regimen lasting 9–12 months was conditionally recommended, although the certainty of evidence was very low. For longer MDR-TB treatment regimens, the guidelines strongly recommended the inclusion of a fluoroquinolone, preferably a later-generation fluoroquinolone, rather than an earlier-generation one. Ethionamide (or prothionamide) was also strongly recommended for use in MDR-TB treatment, despite very low-quality evidence. Regimens should include at least pyrazinamide, a fluoroquinolone, a parenteral agent, ethionamide (or prothionamide), and either cycloserine or p-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) if cycloserine cannot be used. For patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB, a regimen with at least five effective TB medicines during the intensive phase was conditionally recommended. This should include pyrazinamide and four core second-line TB medicines, with at least one from Group A (e.g., levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin), one from Group B (e.g., amikacin, capreomycin, kanamycin), and at least two from Group C (e.g., ethionamide, cycloserine, linezolid, clofazimine). If the minimum number of effective medicines cannot be achieved, agents from Group D2 (e.g., bedaquiline, delamanid) and Group D3 (e.g., PAS, imipenem-cilastatin, meropenem) may be added. The guidelines also conditionally recommended strengthening MDR-TB regimens with high-dose isoniazid and/or ethambutol, although the certainty of evidence was very low. For patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB, elective partial lung resection (lobectomy or wedge resection) may be used alongside a recommended MDR-TB regimen, but this was also a conditional recommendation based on very low-certainty evidence. The 2016 update aimed to revise the 2011 evidence-informed policy recommendations. Unlike the broader scope of the 2011 guidelines, which included programmatic aspects such as rapid diagnostics, patient monitoring, and treatment duration, the 2016 update focused on priority areas such as the optimal combination of medicines for drug-resistant TB, the effectiveness and safety of shorter MDR-TB regimens, the impact of treatment delays, and the role of surgical interventions. The target audience included healthcare providers, program managers, and organizations supporting drug-resistant TB care, with a focus on resource-limited settings. The PICO questions were grouped into four sets addressing these priority areas. Outcomes were defined and scored by the GDG, with mean scores indicating that all outcomes were critical for making recommendations. The certainty of evidence was categorized into four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. Recommendations were classified as strong or conditional based on the balance of desirable and undesirable effects, values, preferences, and resource considerations. These regimens, lasting 9–12 months, showed higher treatment success rates compared to longer regimens in observational studies conducted in Bangladesh, Cameroon, Niger, and other settings. However, the evidence was derived from observational studies, and the certainty was very low. The shorter regimens included an intensive phase of 4–6 months with drugs such as gatifloxacin (or moxifloxacin), kanamycin, prothionamide, clofazimine, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by a continuation phase of 5 months with gatifloxacin (or moxifloxacin), clofazimine, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. The GDG emphasized that the shorter regimen should only be used in its studied form, as modifications could affect its performance. The recommendation was based on data showing a statistically significant higher likelihood of treatment success with shorter regimens compared to longer ones (90% vs. 78% success rates). However, the number of relapses was low, likely due to the limited follow-up of patients. The guidelines also highlighted the importance of considering values, preferences, and feasibility in implementing recommendations. Resource use was assessed from the perspectives of patients and health services, focusing on feasibility and opportunity costs. All recommendations were conditional, reflecting the very low certainty of evidence. The guidelines were reviewed externally, and the final recommendations were disseminated through technical meetings, training activities, and peer-reviewed publications.
